quiz.q: What percentage of a Singapore employee's salary is contributed to CPF (combined employee and employer)?
options: About 20% — similar to European pension systems
37% total (20% employee + 17% employer) — among the world's highest compulsory savings rates
55% total — the majority of salary goes to CPF
quiz.explanation: Singapore's CPF combined contribution rate (employee + employer) reaches 37% for workers under 55 — one of the world's highest compulsory savings rates. This makes Singapore both a high-savings economy (national savings rate 40%+ of GDP) and gives workers a substantial retirement nest egg. The compulsory housing component means most Singapore families own (or co-own with HDB) their homes. Critics note that the system ties up wealth in illiquid housing assets, that minimum sum requirements delay access, and that retirement payouts are modest compared to the amounts contributed. Supporters note Singapore has almost no elderly poverty.

laws.title: Singapore Defamation Law and Political Suits
laws.subtitle: How PAP uses defamation law to manage political opposition
laws.fullDescription: Singapore's defamation law (Defamation Act) follows English common law: false statement of fact published to third party causing reputational damage. Singapore's political culture: PAP leaders have sued opposition politicians, journalists, and foreign newspapers for defamation. Lee Kuan Yew and Lee Hsien Loong both sued critics. The international press (Economist, Far Eastern Economic Review, International Herald Tribune) settled or paid damages after critical reporting. J.B. Jeyaretnam (veteran opposition politician) was financially bankrupted through defamation suits — making him ineligible to run for Parliament. The chilling effect: opposition politicians, journalists, and academics self-censor to avoid defamation suits from well-resourced PAP leaders.
laws.penalty: Defamation: civil damages (potentially bankrupting for individual defendants). Aggravated damages available for deliberate defamation. Criminal defamation: up to 2 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Fair comment on matters of public interest is a defense — but must be genuinely held opinion based on facts
Qualified privilege protects statements made in good faith in certain contexts (parliamentary privilege for MPs)
Truth is a complete defense — but proving truth in political speech is expensive

quiz.q: How has defamation law affected Singapore's opposition politics?
options: Defamation law in Singapore only applies to media — politicians have complete immunity

Opposition politician J.B. Jeyaretnam was financially bankrupted through defamation suits brought by PAP leaders — making him ineligible for Parliament, demonstrating how defamation law can suppress political opposition
Singapore's defamation law has never been used in a political context
PAP lost every defamation suit it brought — courts consistently found political criticism protected
quiz.explanation: J.B. Jeyaretnam — Singapore's most prominent opposition politician, who won the first opposition seat in Parliament in 1981 since independence — was subjected to multiple defamation suits. Cumulative damages and legal costs bankrupted him; under Singapore law, bankrupts cannot stand for Parliament. Jeyaretnam was disqualified from Parliament in 2001 and struggled financially until his death in 2008. His case is cited as an example of 'lawfare' — using legitimate legal tools strategically to eliminate political opponents. The chilling effect on Singapore's remaining opposition and journalists is the lawsuit's broader impact beyond Jeyaretnam himself.

laws.title: Singapore Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act
laws.subtitle: How Singapore legally manages religious sensitivities
laws.fullDescription: Singapore's Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act (MRHA, 1990) empowers the Minister for Home Affairs to issue Restraining Orders against religious leaders who: cause hostility among religions, urge followers to support or oppose political parties, or carry out subversive activities under cover of religion. No court proceedings required — executive order. Presidential Council for Religious Harmony advises. The law reflects Singapore's history: 1964 racial riots, 1969 riots between Chinese and Malay communities. Singapore's approach: CMIO racial categories, Racial Harmony Day (July 21), Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles, and strict management of religious speech. Religious harmony is treated as a security issue requiring preventive intervention.
laws.penalty: Violating Restraining Order: up to 1 year imprisonment. Instigating communal violence on religious grounds: up to 5 years. Causing enmity between religious groups: up to 3 years.
exceptions: Academic study and teaching of comparative religion in universities
Publishing religious texts and conducting regular worship within their faith communities
Interreligious dialogue programs organized with Ministry of Community Development engagement

quiz.q: What power does the MRHA give the Singapore government to manage religious leaders?
options: The MRHA requires all religious leaders to be government-certified before performing duties
The Minister for Home Affairs may issue Restraining Orders against religious leaders who cause inter-religious hostility — without court proceedings
The MRHA bans all non-Buddhist and non-Confucian religions from Singapore
Religious leaders must report their sermons to the government for review 48 hours in advance
quiz.explanation: The Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act gives Singapore's Minister for Home Affairs executive power to issue Restraining Orders against religious leaders who cause inter-religious hostility or mix religion with politics — without requiring a court hearing. The order can limit who the religious leader communicates with and require reporting on activities. This executive-not-judicial approach allows swift action but means no independent review of whether the minister's assessment of 'harm' is accurate. The law has been invoked rarely but its existence shapes religious leaders' speech — a preventive legal architecture for communal harmony management.

laws.title: Singapore Universal Healthcare — 3M Framework
laws.subtitle: Singapore's unique approach to universal healthcare financing
laws.fullDescription: Singapore's healthcare system uses a '3M' framework: Medisave (CPF medical savings account — individuals use their own savings first), MediShield Life (mandatory national health insurance for catastrophic coverage), and Medifund (government safety net for those who cannot afford care). Singapore achieves excellent health outcomes: life expectancy 83.9 years (world's 3rd highest), infant mortality 2.1/1,000. Healthcare spending is 4.5% of GDP — very efficient for outcomes achieved. Singapore's system philosophy: shared individual responsibility (use your Medisave), insurance for catastrophic events (MediShield Life), and state safety net (Medifund). Private and public hospitals coexist. Polyclinics provide subsidized primary care.
laws.penalty: Operating medical facility without MOH license: criminal prosecution. Healthcare fraud (billing Medisave for non-performed services): up to 7 years imprisonment. Medical negligence: civil liability plus SMC (Singapore Medical Council) professional sanctions.
exceptions: Subsidized B2/C ward public hospital treatment is highly subsidized — government covers majority
Medifund covers those who fall through all other payment sources
Emergency treatment must be provided regardless of ability to pay — costs covered by Medifund if necessary

quiz.q: What philosophy underlies Singapore's '3M' healthcare framework?
options: Government pays for all healthcare — individual contributions are token amounts

Shared responsibility: individuals use personal Medisave savings first, then catastrophic insurance (MediShield Life), then government safety net (Medifund) — avoiding free-rider problems while ensuring no one is denied care
Private insurance covers all healthcare — the government only subsidizes premiums
All healthcare is free — Singapore eliminates financial barriers to care through full government funding
quiz.explanation: Singapore's 3M healthcare philosophy is deliberately structured around shared responsibility. By requiring individuals to pay from their personal Medisave (CPF medical savings) first, Singapore avoids the moral hazard of free care — people have an incentive to use healthcare wisely rather than treating it as a free good. MediShield Life insurance protects against catastrophic bills that would bankrupt even careful savers. Medifund catches those who are genuinely unable to pay. This tiered approach — personal savings, insurance, safety net — achieves near-universal coverage efficiently and is studied globally as an alternative to both fully-state and fully-private healthcare models.

laws.title: Singapore Employment Act and Fair Consideration Framework
laws.subtitle: Singapore's employment law and anti-discrimination regulations
laws.fullDescription: Singapore's Employment Act covers most employees (not senior managers, domestic workers, seafarers under separate acts). Tripartite Alliance model: government, employers, unions collaborate on labor policy. Singapore's labor market is flexible: no minimum wage initially (replaced by Progressive Wage Model for specific sectors — cleaning, security, landscape); no statutory redundancy payment beyond Employment Act requirements. The Fair Consideration Framework (FCF, 2014) requires employers with 25+ employees to advertise jobs on national job portal for 14 days before hiring foreigners — ensuring locals are considered. The FCF was created due to concerns about companies systematically preferring foreign workers. Progressive Wage Model mandates minimum wages tied to skills upgrading in specific sectors.
laws.penalty: Wrongful dismissal: compensation award up to 1 year salary. Non-compliance with FCF advertising requirement: MOM investigation and Employment Pass applications scrutinized. Discrimination: Tripartite Alliance complaint process.
exceptions: Jobs advertised internally with genuine business reasons may be exempt from 14-day FCF requirement
Startups with fewer than 25 employees have simplified FCF requirements
Intra-company transfers from multinationals have modified FCF requirements

quiz.q: What does Singapore's 'Fair Consideration Framework' require employers to do before hiring foreign workers?
options: Employers must prove there are no Singaporeans qualified for any position — a very high bar
Employers with 25+ employees must advertise positions on the national job portal for 14 days before hiring a foreigner — to ensure local candidates have been considered
Employers must pay a 'foreign worker levy' to the government for every non-Singaporean hired
Fair Consideration Framework requires 50% of employees in any company to be Singapore citizens
quiz.explanation: Singapore's Fair Consideration Framework (2014) was introduced following complaints that some employers — particularly banks and tech companies with large expatriate workforces — had systematic preferences for foreign workers regardless of qualified local candidates. The FCF requires employers with 25+ employees to advertise any professional, manager, executive, or technician (PMET) job on the national MyCareersFuture portal for 14 days before applying for an Employment Pass for a foreign hire. This doesn't prevent hiring foreigners but ensures Singaporeans have been given the opportunity to apply. Companies with disproportionately few Singaporeans face enhanced scrutiny.
